initial_presentation: A 54-year-old Hispanic man experienced a decline in grip strength, which was followed by weakness in his lower limbs after one year.

A 57-year-old male was admitted to an outside hospital with S-T elevation myocardial infarction (MI). During his stay, he experienced acute hypotension and required emergent central venous access through the right subclavian vein for vasopressors. He was stabilized at the outside facility. Two days later, he exhibited acute left hemiplegia and right gaze deviation. Transfer to our facility was arranged. During transport, he had a focal seizure and was intubated for airway protection. In the emergency department, his Glasgow coma scale score was 10 (E: 4, V: 1, M: 5). He was opening his eyes spontaneously. He had a right gaze deviation. He was localizing with the right lower and upper extremities but was plegic on the left side of his body. He experienced a cluster of seizures and was started on levetiracetam and propofol infusion.

A 17-year-old girl presented with a primary concern of retained deciduous teeth. Physical examination showed short stature, prominent frontal and parietal regions, a depressed nasal bridge, a beaked nose, underdeveloped midface, an obtuse mandibular gonial angle with relative prognathism, wrinkled skin over the fingertips, and nail abnormalities. Intraoral examination identified a deep midline antero-posterior ridge of the palate, a high arched palate, multiple retained deciduous teeth with caries, crowding, and enamel hypoplasia.

A 49-year-old African American female with a history of chronic allergic rhinitis, fibroids, and normocytic anemia came to the emergency room with chest pain lasting 10 days. The pain was sharp, rated four out of 10, located mid-sternally, non-radiating, and worsened with deep breaths and movements. She also experienced malaise, chills, fatigue, and reported a subjective fever for a week, along with right-sided sinus pressure and nosebleeds. She performed nasal irrigation four times daily after experiencing nasal congestion and nosebleeds. After three days of nasal irrigation, she noted worsening fatigue and subjective fevers. Upon arrival at the emergency room, she had intermittent fever episodes with a peak temperature of 103.1°F, managed with acetaminophen. She remained afebrile during her hospital stay after starting antibiotics. In the emergency department, she had sinus tachycardia at 110 beats per minute, which improved after fluid resuscitation with lactated ringers.

The patient is a two-year-old girl born at full term to consanguineous Saudi parents via cesarean section due to breech presentation. She has a history of poor sucking, hypotonia, bilateral ptosis, and recurrent admissions to the pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) for apnea. The family history is unremarkable. The clinical course began with a sudden cessation of breathing lasting more than 15 minutes, followed by a three-minute arrest. She also has a history of choking and coughing. Upon examination, the patient was afebrile, dehydrated, and pale, with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 3. Stabilization efforts were initiated, and she was intubated in the PICU.

A 40-year-old Filipino male presented with a three-month history of reduced vision in his right eye. The patient had a known allergic hypersensitivity to fluorescein, with no other significant medical or ocular history. He did not have systemic conditions such as hypertension, diabetes mellitus, or hypercholesterolemia. There was no history of retinal detachment, radiation exposure, intraocular inflammation, tapetoretinal degeneration, or vascular occlusion. His family history was unremarkable, and he was not taking any medications or using illicit drugs.

A 31-year-old male reported experiencing abdominal pain that had intensified over the past 3 months. He had been dealing with intermittent epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting for the past year. The recent increase in abdominal pain prompted him to seek medical attention. Additionally, he experienced a weight loss of 2 kg over the past month. He was found to have partial gut obstruction. During an exploratory laparotomy, a 10-cm mass was discovered in the duodenal region, situated in the retroperitoneal area near the aorta. A gastrojejunostomy was performed, but the mass was not removed due to the high risk of aortic injury.

A 33-year-old African American male presented with multiple nodular skin lesions, primarily located in the axilla and inguinal areas. He reported an increase in the number and size of draining pustules. The patient also experienced generalized joint pains, including swelling and redness in the left knee and right elbow. These symptoms typically occur 1 to 2 times yearly and subside with antibiotic treatment. On skin examination, generalized suppurate nodules and chronic scars were observed, along with sinus tracts in the intertriginous areas. Joint examination revealed effusions in the ankles, knees, elbows, wrists, and digits, with a notable swelling in the right second phalanx.

A 3-year-old male child, born to parents who are not related by blood, presented with three slow-growing, painless, hard masses on the outer aspect of the right leg, first noticed at 2 months of age. The child was delivered at full term without any congenital abnormalities. Over time, he developed multiple asymptomatic, solid, elevated, skin-colored lesions that eventually merged into larger hard masses. The child had a history of low birth weight and delayed gross motor development milestones, but exhibited no mental retardation or gait abnormalities. There was no history of trauma, prior inflammation, or similar lesions in family members. Physical examination revealed a single large, non-tender, subcutaneous hard mass measuring 4 cm × 5 cm on the anterolateral aspect of the right thigh, with the skin over the lesion being pinchable. Additionally, there were two smaller lesions measuring 2 cm × 3 cm and 2 cm × 2 cm on the outer aspect of the right lower leg, with the surface showing atrophy and scaling. No other skeletal deformities were observed.

A 27-year-old female with a history of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, systemic lupus erythematosus, and end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis was admitted for acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding. Upper and lower endoscopies were planned.
